chicken vaccine on 20 November 2026 India 18.11.2026 586 India plans to introduce its first domestically developed vaccine against highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in chickens. Developed by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD), it is scheduled to be formally dedicated to the nation by agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on 20 November 2026. The vaccine targets H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a, which the announcement identifies as the strain responsible for most bird-flu outbreaks in chickens. ICAR-NIHSAD, based in Bhopal, developed the product through its work on high-security animal diseases. No commercial vaccine specifically targeting this strain had previously been available. The institute operates under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, whose institutions conduct research on emerging animal-health threats. India has recorded more than 500 outbreaks involving the H5N1 and H5N8 subtypes combined since avian influenza was first detected in the country in 2006. Highly pathogenic avian influenza can kill nearly all infected birds. Control measures, including large-scale culling and restrictions on animal movements, can also interrupt poultry commerce within India and across its borders. Direct and indirect losses associated with India's 2006 outbreak were estimated at approximately 22 billion–30 billion rupees. The economic effects of poultry outbreaks extend beyond producers to businesses supplying feed, processing birds and distributing or selling poultry products. Disease-control restrictions can also limit access to markets for agricultural businesses. The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare estimates that a major bird-flu outbreak could reduce India's GDP growth by up to 1.5%. It also estimates that more than 20% of the national poultry population could be at risk if infection spreads without effective controls. These estimates form part of the government's account of the economic and animal-health risks associated with the disease. Infections involving H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a have been detected in several animal species, including mammals. The government announcement also cites three human infections associated with this strain. Its discussion of livestock biosecurity covers farms where dairy cattle and poultry are kept together or nearby, including hygiene procedures, controls on animal movements and separation of different animal populations. Globally, World Health Organization figures cited by the ministry put the number of reported human H5N1 infections since 2003 at 1,003 across 25 countries, including 479 deaths. The figures cover human H5N1 infections, while the three strain-specific cases cited in the announcement concern Clade 2.3.2.1a. chicken vaccine on 20 November 2026 India 18.11.2026 586 India plans to introduce its first domestically developed vaccine against highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in chickens. Developed by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD), it is scheduled to be formally dedicated to the nation by agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on 20 November 2026. The vaccine targets H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a, which the announcement identifies as the strain responsible for most bird-flu outbreaks in chickens. ICAR-NIHSAD, based in Bhopal, developed the product through its work on high-security animal diseases. No commercial vaccine specifically targeting this strain had previously been available. The institute operates under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, whose institutions conduct research on emerging animal-health threats. India has recorded more than 500 outbreaks involving the H5N1 and H5N8 subtypes combined since avian influenza was first detected in the country in 2006. Highly pathogenic avian influenza can kill nearly all infected birds. Control measures, including large-scale culling and restrictions on animal movements, can also interrupt poultry commerce within India and across its borders. Direct and indirect losses associated with India's 2006 outbreak were estimated at approximately 22 billion–30 billion rupees. The economic effects of poultry outbreaks extend beyond producers to businesses supplying feed, processing birds and distributing or selling poultry products. Disease-control restrictions can also limit access to markets for agricultural businesses. The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare estimates that a major bird-flu outbreak could reduce India's GDP growth by up to 1.5%. It also estimates that more than 20% of the national poultry population could be at risk if infection spreads without effective controls. These estimates form part of the government's account of the economic and animal-health risks associated with the disease. Infections involving H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a have been detected in several animal species, including mammals. The government announcement also cites three human infections associated with this strain. Its discussion of livestock biosecurity covers farms where dairy cattle and poultry are kept together or nearby, including hygiene procedures, controls on animal movements and separation of different animal populations. Globally, World Health Organization figures cited by the ministry put the number of reported human H5N1 infections since 2003 at 1,003 across 25 countries, including 479 deaths. The figures cover human H5N1 infections, while the three strain-specific cases cited in the announcement concern Clade 2.3.2.1a. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Ginsenoside Rg1 Adjuvant Boosts Immune Protection Against H9N2 Avian Influenza in Chickens by November 14, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Ginsenoside Rg1 Adjuvant Boosts Immune Protection Against H9N2 Avian Influenza in Chickens Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers investigating novel poultry immunization strategies have demonstrated that supplementing an inactivated H9N2 avian influenza vaccine with ginsenoside Rg1 substantially enhances immune responses and protective efficacy in young chickens. In a controlled trial conducted using one-day-old non-immunized Arbor Acres broiler chicks, administering ginsenoside Rg1 alongside the standard inactivated H9N2 vaccine generated significantly higher levels of specific immunoglobulins and hemagglutination inhibition titers compared to vaccination alone. Following an experimental intranasal viral challenge with live avian influenza, birds that received the adjuvant regimen exhibited marked reductions in oropharyngeal and cloacal viral shedding, alongside lower viral loads within critical respiratory and renal tissues. These findings indicate that ginsenoside Rg1 holds strong potential as an effective natural adjuvant for avian influenza vaccination programs. The global poultry sector faces persistent operational and economic setbacks driven by the continuous circulation of the H9N2 subtype, which represents the most widespread form of low pathogenic avian influenza found in domestic bird populations. More critically, ongoing genomic monitoring reveals that circulating H9N2 lineages continuously undergo antigenic variation and genetic reassortment within agricultural reservoirs. Through these evolutionary shifts, H9N2 strains frequently donate essential internal genetic segments to emerging highly pathogenic avian influenza variants, including lethal subtypes such as H5N1 and H7N9. This genetic exchange significantly amplifies the risk of interspecies transmission and poses ongoing zoonotic threats to human public health. To counteract widespread circulation, agricultural operations in numerous countries, including China, South Korea, and Egypt, routinely administer oil-adjuvanted inactivated vaccines to poultry flocks. Nevertheless, recurrent field outbreaks persist even among heavily vaccinated bird populations, exposing critical shortcomings in current immunization programs that largely stem from the limited antigenic breadth and suboptimal immunogenicity of existing formulations. Vaccine effectiveness depends fundamentally not only on target antigen selection but also on the pharmacological properties of the adjuvant used to stimulate the host immune system. While commercial animal vaccines commonly incorporate adjuvants such as Matrix-M, CpG1018, MF59, or traditional aluminum salts, these agents present notable practical limitations. Many conventional formulations fail to generate adequate cellular immune activation, carry potential risks of adverse reactions, or induce pronounced local tissue irritation at injection sites. These recognized biological drawbacks highlight an urgent need in veterinary medicine to identify safe, non-toxic adjuvants capable of enhancing cellular and humoral protection without compromising animal welfare. In the search for safer alternatives, natural pharmacological compounds derived from traditional botanical medicine have attracted growing scientific attention due to their low intrinsic toxicity, high biocompatibility, and diverse immunomodulatory capabilities. Previous immunological studies have established that ginsenoside Rg1 possesses the capacity to stimulate balanced T helper type 1 and T helper type 2 immune responses in multiple animal species. Scientific literature has documented its adjuvant efficacy in experimental vaccination models against several major animal and human viral pathogens, including hepatitis B virus, infectious bursal disease virus, influenza, and porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus. However, despite these encouraging demonstrations in other disease contexts, the functional capacity of ginsenoside Rg1 to bolster protective immunity against avian H9N2 influenza in commercial poultry had remained entirely unexplored prior to this comprehensive study. To rigorously evaluate the adjuvant capabilities of the compound, the research team procured high-grade ginsenoside Rg1 possessing a verified chemical purity exceeding 98 percent from a specialized biochemical supplier in Chengdu, China. Recognizing that bacterial endotoxin contamination can confound immunological evaluations by introducing uncontrolled inflammatory artifacts, the investigators processed the saponin solution through a dedicated gel endotoxin-removal column, successfully verifying that residual endotoxin concentrations remained strictly below 0.5 endotoxin units per milliliter. The viral component utilized throughout the immunization and challenge trials was the low pathogenic avian influenza serotype strain designated A/Chicken/Jilin/DH109/2012, which was propagated and adapted in nine-day-old specific-pathogen-free embryonated chicken eggs. Commercial inactivated H9N2 vaccines were acquired from Harbin Pharmaceutical Group Biological Vaccine Company. The experimental cohort comprised 150 one-day-old non-immunized Arbor Acres chicks obtained from a certified commercial hatchery, which were randomly divided into three identical treatment groups of 50 chicks each to establish rigorous comparative baselines under approved institutional animal care protocols. The experimental protocol evaluated three distinct cohorts: an unadjuvanted vaccine group, an Rg1-supplemented vaccine group, and an unvaccinated control group receiving sterile phosphate-buffered saline. Birds in both vaccinated groups were administered 200 microliters of the inactivated H9N2 vaccine by intramuscular injection on three occasions spaced exactly two weeks apart, on days 0, 14, and 28. Concurrently with the initial immunization, the adjuvant group received ginsenoside Rg1 dissolved in drinking water at a calculated dosage of 1 milligram per kilogram of body weight daily for seven consecutive days. Within each 50-bird group, specific biological replicates were systematically assigned to pre-planned investigative endpoints: ten live chickens were monitored longitudinally for blood serum antibodies and mucosal swabs; 18 were sampled across scheduled intervals for splenic lymphocyte proliferation assays; five were evaluated for immune organ weights; five underwent hepatic and renal histopathological examination; nine were assessed for organ viral loads; and 13 were observed continuously for clinical health signs, body weight development, and survival. Humoral immune responses were tracked by collecting serum samples on days 14, 28, and 42 following the initial vaccination to measure specific immunoglobulin G concentrations and hemagglutination inhibition titers. Enzymatic analysis revealed that while the standard vaccine induced detectable antibodies above control levels, the addition of ginsenoside Rg1 produced a marked enhancement in antibody production. By days 28 and 42, specific serum immunoglobulin G levels were significantly elevated in the Rg1 combination group relative to birds receiving the unadjuvanted vaccine (p < 0.05). Furthermore, hemagglutination inhibition titers in the adjuvant group displayed a sustained, statistically significant rise throughout the 42-day observation window. Because a hemagglutination inhibition titer of at least 4 log2 is widely recognized as the definitive benchmark required for neutralizing viral particles, preventing hemagglutinin-receptor binding, and blocking viral transmission, the robust titers achieved in the Rg1 cohort underscore the compound’s capacity to amplify protective neutralizing antibody synthesis. Beyond antibody production, the researchers assessed cell-mediated immunity, which plays a pivotal role in clearing intracellular viral infections and establishing durable immunological memory. Splenic lymphocytes harvested on days 14, 28, and 42 post-immunization were tested using Cell Counting Kit-8 colorimetric assays to evaluate proliferation dynamics. At days 28 and 42, lymphocytes isolated from chicks receiving ginsenoside Rg1 exhibited significantly higher proliferative responses compared to the vaccine-only group (p < 0.05). Complementary multi-parameter flow cytometry revealed that the proportions of both CD3+CD4+ helper T cells and CD3+CD8+ cytotoxic T cells were markedly expanded in the Rg1 group relative to controls. In parallel, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays showed that the adjuvant regimen significantly enhanced serum concentrations of key regulatory cytokines, including interferon-gamma, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-4, and interleukin-6. This coordinated upregulation demonstrates that ginsenoside Rg1 simultaneously potentiates cytotoxic CD8+ cellular effector pathways and promotes Th2-associated cytokine production responsible for directing optimal B-cell maturation. The investigation also confirmed that ginsenoside Rg1 supplementation supported healthy lymphoid organ development without inducing systemic organ toxicity. On day 28 post-inoculation, chickens in the adjuvant cohort exhibited significantly increased weight indices for the spleen, thymus, and bursa of Fabricius compared to those receiving vaccine alone. Biochemical screening of serum alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase revealed no abnormal deviations, while histopathological examination of liver and kidney sections demonstrated normal tissue architecture without pathological lesions across all vaccinated groups. Fourteen days following the final immunization, birds were challenged intranasally with 100 microliters containing 10^7 median egg infectious doses of the live H9N2 strain. Swab sampling assessed by quantitative real-time PCR revealed that while unvaccinated controls exhibited 90 percent shedding rates at day 14 and vaccine-only birds shed virus through day 10, the Rg1 group completely cleared oropharyngeal and cloacal shedding by day 10. Moreover, tissue viral load assessments confirmed that live virus was undetectable in the lungs and kidneys of Rg1-treated chickens by day 10 post-challenge. In evaluating the overall outcomes, the authors noted that combining oral ginsenoside Rg1 with an inactivated H9N2 vaccine successfully stimulated both branches of the avian adaptive immune system, resulting in accelerated viral clearance and superior tissue protection. The botanical adjuvant enhanced the production of protective neutralizing antibodies, expanded functional T-cell subsets, and bolstered key cytokine networks while maintaining an excellent biosafety profile. Nonetheless, the researchers explicitly acknowledged two important methodological limitations in their experimental design. First, the toxicological screening was restricted to targeted liver and kidney biochemistry and histopathology, rather than an exhaustive safety assessment adhering strictly to international World Health Organization or European Medicines Agency regulatory standards. Second, the study did not incorporate an isolated control cohort receiving ginsenoside Rg1 monotherapy without vaccination, precluding direct observation of the adjuvant’s baseline physiological effects in unimmunized animals. Thursday, November 19, 2026 The NERC 2026-2027 Winter (Electrical Grid) Reliability Assessment NERC 2026-2027 WRA Snapshot #19,421 It is the job of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) to "ensure the reliability of the North American bulk power system", a mandate given to it in 2006 as a result of the 2003 Northeast blackout which affected more than 50 million people in the United States and Ontario, Canada. In the fall of 2024, a preprint (see Establishing Nationwide Power System Vulnerability Index across US Counties Using Interpretable Machine Learning) - later published in Applied Energy - warned on the increasing vulnerability of of the U.S. power grid over the past decade. They identified `. . . 318 counties across 45 states as hotspots for high power system vulnerability, particularly in the West Coast (California and Washington), the East Coast (Florida and the Northeast area), the Great Lakes megalopolis (Chicago-Detroit metropolitan areas), and the Gulf of Mexico (Texas)' In the summer of 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy published a 73-page report that warned that if current schedules for retirement of reliable power generation (especially baseload) continue, without enough firm replacement, the risk of blackouts in 2030 could increase by 100× over current levels. Number one on their Key Takeaways is: Status Quo is Unsustainable. The status quo of more generation retirements and less dependable replacement generation is neither consistent with winning the AI race and ensuring affordable energy for all Americans, nor with continued grid reliability (ensuring “resource adequacy”). Absent intervention, it is impossible for the nation’s bulk power system to meet the AI growth requirements while maintaining a reliable power grid and keeping energy costs low for our citizens. Their words, not mine. Ten months ago, in NERC: Long-Term Reliability Assessment (Jan 2026), we looked at a 181-page NERC Long-Term Reliability Report which similarly warned that our power grid is facing a growing risk of electrical shortfalls over the next decade. From their press release: January 29, 2026 WASHINGTON, D.C. – NERC’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (LTRA) and infographic spotlight intensifying resource adequacy risks throughout the North American bulk power system (BPS) over the next 10 years. Summer peak demand is forecast to grow by 224 GW, a more than 69% increase over the 2024 LTRA forecast with new data centers for artificial intelligence and the digital economy accounting for most of the projected increase. Winter demand growth continues to outpace summer demand growth with 246 GW of growth forecast over the next 10 years, reflecting the evolution of electricity usage. Uncertainty and lag in the pace of new resource additions are driving heightened concerns that industry will not be able to keep up with rapidly increasing demand. In addition to ageing infrastructure, and ever increasing power demands, there are threats from cyber attacks (see DHS: NIAC Cyber Threat Report), solar flares and CMEs (see FEMA: Preparing the Nation for Space Weather Events), and even potential disruptions due to earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis. These are serious enough threats that in December of 2018, in NIAC: Surviving A Catastrophic Power Outage, we looked at a NIAC (National Infrastructure Advisory Council) 94-page report that examined the United State's current ability to respond to and recover from a widespread catastrophic power outage. While we've avoided catastrophic failures thus far, the margins for error get narrower every year, and it has required repeated emergency actions - such as the following, issued yesterday by the U.S. Department of Energy - to keep the power flowing. Energy Secretary Acts to Protect Mid-Atlantic Grid Secretary Wright issues emergency order to stabilize the mid-Atlantic grid and minimize the risk of energy shortfalls in 13 states and the District of Columbia. Energy.gov November 18, 2026 WASHINGTON—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright issued an emergency order to reduce the risk of power outages and strengthen grid reliability across the mid-Atlantic region. The order permits PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM), in coordination with Talen Energy Corporation, to run Unit 4 at the Wagner Generating Station in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, to meet anticipated electricity demand. The order follows an application from PJM submitted on October 23, 2026. (Continue . . . ) Yesterday (Nov 18th) NERC released their annual winter reliability assessment (63-page PDF), which identifies this year's record El Niño as a genuine wildcard. NERC’s 2026–2027 Winter Reliability Assessment (WRA) finds that resource additions, delayed retirements and better generator performance in cold weather have improved the overall reliability outlook for the upcoming winter. However, while all areas are assessed as having adequate resources for normal winter peak load, extreme wide-area winter conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls. Furthermore, this year’s El Niño weather system, which introduces an additional layer of unpredictability, may also cause disruption. You'll find a more detailed description in their news release. Increasing Demand and El Niño Challenge Winter Grid Reliability November 18, 2026 WASHINGTON, D.C. – NERC’s 2026–2027 Winter Reliability Assessment (WRA) finds that resource additions, delayed retirements and better generator performance in cold weather have improved the overall reliability outlook for the upcoming winter. However, while all areas are assessed as having adequate resources for normal winter peak load, extreme wide-area winter conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls. Furthermore, this year’s El Niño weather system, which introduces an additional layer of unpredictability, may also cause disruption. System operators and energy officials are encouraged to become familiar with the recommendations in the 2026–2027 WRA and the joint FERC, NERC and Regional Entities’ Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period System Performance Review and visit NERC’s new Cold Weather Risk Mitigation web page to help prepare and operate reliably in potentially extreme winter conditions. Although recent reports from NERC and the ERO Enterprise highlight measurable improvements in industry’s cold-weather performance largely due to improved preparation and the implementation of freeze protection measures, NERC President and Chief Executive Officer Jim Robb cautioned, “While the resource outlook has improved, the unpredictable weather of El Niño and rapid load growth present unique challenges this winter. We anticipate operators will need everything in their tool kit—including requests for emergency support—to maintain reliable operations.” (Continue . . . ) In February of 2021, 3 successive winter storms swept across Texas, Louisiana, and Oklahoma, causing the worst collapse of the Texas energy grid on record (see Texas: The Latest - But Not The Last - Grid Down Crisis). At least 4.5 million homes were without power during bitter winter temperatures - some for a week - resulting in hundreds of deaths and tens of billions of dollars of damage (see City of Austin & Travis County 2021 WINTER STORM URI AFTER-ACTION REVIEW). While no one can pinpoint when or where the next major grid failure will occur, it is well worth preparing for such an eventuality, particularly if you live in the colder regions of the country. Now is the time to figure out how you and your family will stay warm, and cook, and cope should your power go out for a week or more. Some resources to help you get started include: CDC Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm Ready.gov #WinterReady Wednesday, November 18, 2026 One Health: Severe H9N2 virus infection in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure Credit Wikipedia #19,420 Eight days ago, in HK CHP Reports 6 H9N2 Cases over the past 4 Reporting Periods, we looked at the latest batch of H9N2 reported from the Chinese mainland. Again this week, in what it getting to be almost a weekly occurrence, WHO WPRO announced yet another case, this time in Hunan Province. Human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus From 6 to 12 November 2026, one new case of human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus was reported from China to WHO in the Western Pacific Region. The case is a paediatric patient from Hunan Province, with symptom onset on 20 October 2026. The case had exposure to household poultry, and one of the environmental samples tested positive for influenza A(H9). All close contacts of the case have tested negative for influenza A. The case has now recovered. Since 2015, a total of 190 cases of human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2), including two deaths (both with underlying conditions), have been reported to WHO in the Western Pacific Region. Of these, 187 were reported from China, two were from Cambodia, and one was from Viet Nam. Most human infections with avian influenza A(H9N2) have been associated with exposure to infected poultry or contaminated poultry environments, and the majority of cases have been mild. Sporadic human infections continue to be expected in areas where H9N2 viruses circulate in poultry populations. Current evidence indicates that H9N2 viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission, and the risk of further community-level spread remains low. While most reported cases have been in children, China is more likely to detect pediatric cases - particularly those hospitalized in major urban centers - as those cohorts are often prioritized for testing for novel flu. Adult cases, many of whom are unlikely to seek medical care, are believed more likely to go undetected. H9N2 is ubiquitous in Chinese poultry, and attempts to control the disease via largely ineffective vaccines has led to silent transmission (see NPJ Vaccines: Impact of Inactivated Vaccine on Transmission and Evolution of H9N2 Avian Influenza Virus in Chickens). Complicating matters, as an LPAI (low path avian influenza), H9N2 is not considered a `reportable' disease by WOAH (formerly the OIE), even though it is zoonotic. We've seen seroprevalence studies which suggest people with exposure to infected poultry often develop H9 antibodies, suggesting mild or asymptomatic infection. As a result we are probably only seeing the tip of the H9N2 pyramid, as is true with most infectious diseases in the community. All of which brings us to a new report in One Health, which describes the unexpected finding of an H9N2 infection in an elderly patient already hospitalized for 10 days in Guangzhou for complications from chemotherapy (see timeline below). The patient reportedly had no exposure to poultry, and was only diagnosed because worsening pulmonary function led doctors to order metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of a bronchial lavage sample. It detected both bacterial and H9 viral infection. Of note, subsequent whole gene sequencing (WGS) found several markers linked to mammalian adaptation, including: HA Q226L (human-type receptor binding). PB2 L89V and I292V (increased polymerase activity; I292V also dampens the interferon response). Beyond these findings, this is a reminder of how easily cases can fly under the radar, even those who are already hospitalized for unrelated conditions. First some excerpts from this report, after which I'll have a brief postscript. Severe H9N2 virus infection in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure: implications for surveillance of unexplained severe pneumonia Jingjing Zhang a 1, Weijia Wang b 1, Dan Xia a 1, Yifan Pan c, Yiyun Chen a, Peiwen Liu a, Yuqian Wu a, Anna Wang a, Tengfei Zhou a, Xia Tao a, Shuiping Hou a, Pingting Zhu a, Yanhui Liu a, Xinwei Wu a, Pengzhe Qin a 2, Zhoubin Zhang a 2, Lan Cao a c 2 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.onehlt.2026.101670Get rights and contentView Under a Creative Commons license Open access Highlights • Severe human H9N2 infection detected without known poultry exposure. • Phylogenetic analysis clusters virus with local strains and a recent human case. • Key molecular markers linked to human adaptation of H9N2 identified. • Highlights gaps in current surveillance for sporadic or atypical H9N2 infections Abstract Objectives To describe a severe human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure and to evaluate implications for surveillance and public health preparedness. Methods Unbiased metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid for initial pathogen detection, and influenza A(H9N2) virus infection was subsequently confirmed by H9N2-specific real-time RT-PCR. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on H9N2-positive respiratory specimens with sufficient viral RNA, followed by phylogenetic analyses to determine the virus genotype and its genetic relationship with local environmental H9N2 viruses and previously reported human H9N2 viruses. Results The virus, A/Guangzhou/23127/2025 (H9N2), belonged to the G57 genotype, with its HA gene classified within lineage B, clade B4.7, according to the recently proposed global A/H9 classification system. Phylogenetic analysis revealed close genetic relationships with local environmental strains. Conclusion Severe H9N2 infection can occur in individuals without known poultry exposure. These findings underscore the need for NGS-based surveillance among hospitalized patients with severe respiratory disease and highlight the importance of strengthening public health strategies to detect sporadic or atypical zoonotic influenza infections. (SNIP) . . . These findings suggest that H9/H9N2 viruses continued to circulate in local poultry-related environments and that human exposure risk persisted during the study period. However, no human H9N2 infections were identified through routine sentinel surveillance in either hospital-based or occupational monitoring programs during the same period. This discrepancy suggests that current surveillance strategies may not be sufficiently sensitive for detecting sporadic human H9N2 infections, especially among patients without recognized poultry exposure or typical influenza-like illness. (SNIP) In conclusion, this severe human H9N2 infection occurred against a background of continued local environmental circulation and occupational exposure risk. These observations also emphasize the public health importance of sustained environmental surveillance, serological monitoring of occupationally exposed populations, and long-term molecular surveillance of H9N2 viruses. Continued genomic monitoring is particularly important for detecting viral genetic changes associated with mammalian adaptation, including mutations that may affect receptor-binding properties or replication in mammalian hosts. (Continue . . . ) In 2024 the ECDC issued guidance for member nations on Enhanced Influenza Surveillance to Detect Avian Influenza Virus Infections in the EU/EEA During the Inter-Seasonal Period., which cautioned: Sentinel surveillance systems are important for the monitoring of respiratory viruses in the EU/EEA, but these systems are not designed and are not sufficiently sensitive to identify a newly emerging virus such as avian influenza in the general population early enough for the purpose of implementing control measures in a timely way. In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza should be subtyped within 24 hours. How rigorously this is followed isn't known. Last month's Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping focused primarily on testing those with known risk exposures. A sobering reminder that, while we comfort ourselves with our current low number of human novel flu detections, we are probably seeing something less than the whole picture. It isn't clear from this announcement exactly where on the zoo grounds this goose was found, or even when. First the Zoo's announcement, followed by reports from other sources. Confirmatory testing at a federal lab is pending. None of the Zoo’s birds are currently showing clinical signs of the disease. The Zoo remains open, with temporary closures limited to a handful of bird habitats. Thursday, November 19, 2026 The NERC 2026-2027 Winter (Electrical Grid) Reliability Assessment NERC 2026-2027 WRA Snapshot #19,421 It is the job of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) to "ensure the reliability of the North American bulk power system", a mandate given to it in 2006 as a result of the 2003 Northeast blackout which affected more than 50 million people in the United States and Ontario, Canada. In the fall of 2024, a preprint (see Establishing Nationwide Power System Vulnerability Index across US Counties Using Interpretable Machine Learning) - later published in Applied Energy - warned on the increasing vulnerability of of the U.S. power grid over the past decade. They identified `. . . 318 counties across 45 states as hotspots for high power system vulnerability, particularly in the West Coast (California and Washington), the East Coast (Florida and the Northeast area), the Great Lakes megalopolis (Chicago-Detroit metropolitan areas), and the Gulf of Mexico (Texas)' In the summer of 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy published a 73-page report that warned that if current schedules for retirement of reliable power generation (especially baseload) continue, without enough firm replacement, the risk of blackouts in 2030 could increase by 100× over current levels. Number one on their Key Takeaways is: Status Quo is Unsustainable. The status quo of more generation retirements and less dependable replacement generation is neither consistent with winning the AI race and ensuring affordable energy for all Americans, nor with continued grid reliability (ensuring “resource adequacy”). Absent intervention, it is impossible for the nation’s bulk power system to meet the AI growth requirements while maintaining a reliable power grid and keeping energy costs low for our citizens. Their words, not mine. Ten months ago, in NERC: Long-Term Reliability Assessment (Jan 2026), we looked at a 181-page NERC Long-Term Reliability Report which similarly warned that our power grid is facing a growing risk of electrical shortfalls over the next decade. From their press release: January 29, 2026 WASHINGTON, D.C. – NERC’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (LTRA) and infographic spotlight intensifying resource adequacy risks throughout the North American bulk power system (BPS) over the next 10 years. Summer peak demand is forecast to grow by 224 GW, a more than 69% increase over the 2024 LTRA forecast with new data centers for artificial intelligence and the digital economy accounting for most of the projected increase. Winter demand growth continues to outpace summer demand growth with 246 GW of growth forecast over the next 10 years, reflecting the evolution of electricity usage. Uncertainty and lag in the pace of new resource additions are driving heightened concerns that industry will not be able to keep up with rapidly increasing demand. In addition to ageing infrastructure, and ever increasing power demands, there are threats from cyber attacks (see DHS: NIAC Cyber Threat Report), solar flares and CMEs (see FEMA: Preparing the Nation for Space Weather Events), and even potential disruptions due to earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis. These are serious enough threats that in December of 2018, in NIAC: Surviving A Catastrophic Power Outage, we looked at a NIAC (National Infrastructure Advisory Council) 94-page report that examined the United State's current ability to respond to and recover from a widespread catastrophic power outage. While we've avoided catastrophic failures thus far, the margins for error get narrower every year, and it has required repeated emergency actions - such as the following, issued yesterday by the U.S. Department of Energy - to keep the power flowing. Energy Secretary Acts to Protect Mid-Atlantic Grid Secretary Wright issues emergency order to stabilize the mid-Atlantic grid and minimize the risk of energy shortfalls in 13 states and the District of Columbia. Energy.gov November 18, 2026 WASHINGTON—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright issued an emergency order to reduce the risk of power outages and strengthen grid reliability across the mid-Atlantic region. The order permits PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM), in coordination with Talen Energy Corporation, to run Unit 4 at the Wagner Generating Station in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, to meet anticipated electricity demand. The order follows an application from PJM submitted on October 23, 2026. (Continue . . . ) Yesterday (Nov 18th) NERC released their annual winter reliability assessment (63-page PDF), which identifies this year's record El Niño as a genuine wildcard. NERC’s 2026–2027 Winter Reliability Assessment (WRA) finds that resource additions, delayed retirements and better generator performance in cold weather have improved the overall reliability outlook for the upcoming winter. However, while all areas are assessed as having adequate resources for normal winter peak load, extreme wide-area winter conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls. Furthermore, this year’s El Niño weather system, which introduces an additional layer of unpredictability, may also cause disruption. You'll find a more detailed description in their news release. Increasing Demand and El Niño Challenge Winter Grid Reliability November 18, 2026 WASHINGTON, D.C. – NERC’s 2026–2027 Winter Reliability Assessment (WRA) finds that resource additions, delayed retirements and better generator performance in cold weather have improved the overall reliability outlook for the upcoming winter. However, while all areas are assessed as having adequate resources for normal winter peak load, extreme wide-area winter conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls. Furthermore, this year’s El Niño weather system, which introduces an additional layer of unpredictability, may also cause disruption. System operators and energy officials are encouraged to become familiar with the recommendations in the 2026–2027 WRA and the joint FERC, NERC and Regional Entities’ Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period System Performance Review and visit NERC’s new Cold Weather Risk Mitigation web page to help prepare and operate reliably in potentially extreme winter conditions. Although recent reports from NERC and the ERO Enterprise highlight measurable improvements in industry’s cold-weather performance largely due to improved preparation and the implementation of freeze protection measures, NERC President and Chief Executive Officer Jim Robb cautioned, “While the resource outlook has improved, the unpredictable weather of El Niño and rapid load growth present unique challenges this winter. We anticipate operators will need everything in their tool kit—including requests for emergency support—to maintain reliable operations.” (Continue . . . ) In February of 2021, 3 successive winter storms swept across Texas, Louisiana, and Oklahoma, causing the worst collapse of the Texas energy grid on record (see Texas: The Latest - But Not The Last - Grid Down Crisis). At least 4.5 million homes were without power during bitter winter temperatures - some for a week - resulting in hundreds of deaths and tens of billions of dollars of damage (see City of Austin & Travis County 2021 WINTER STORM URI AFTER-ACTION REVIEW). While no one can pinpoint when or where the next major grid failure will occur, it is well worth preparing for such an eventuality, particularly if you live in the colder regions of the country. Now is the time to figure out how you and your family will stay warm, and cook, and cope should your power go out for a week or more. Some resources to help you get started include: CDC Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm Ready.gov #WinterReady Wednesday, November 18, 2026 One Health: Severe H9N2 virus infection in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure Credit Wikipedia #19,420 Eight days ago, in HK CHP Reports 6 H9N2 Cases over the past 4 Reporting Periods, we looked at the latest batch of H9N2 reported from the Chinese mainland. Again this week, in what it getting to be almost a weekly occurrence, WHO WPRO announced yet another case, this time in Hunan Province. Human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus From 6 to 12 November 2026, one new case of human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus was reported from China to WHO in the Western Pacific Region. The case is a paediatric patient from Hunan Province, with symptom onset on 20 October 2026. The case had exposure to household poultry, and one of the environmental samples tested positive for influenza A(H9). All close contacts of the case have tested negative for influenza A. The case has now recovered. Since 2015, a total of 190 cases of human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2), including two deaths (both with underlying conditions), have been reported to WHO in the Western Pacific Region. Of these, 187 were reported from China, two were from Cambodia, and one was from Viet Nam. Most human infections with avian influenza A(H9N2) have been associated with exposure to infected poultry or contaminated poultry environments, and the majority of cases have been mild. Sporadic human infections continue to be expected in areas where H9N2 viruses circulate in poultry populations. Current evidence indicates that H9N2 viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission, and the risk of further community-level spread remains low. While most reported cases have been in children, China is more likely to detect pediatric cases - particularly those hospitalized in major urban centers - as those cohorts are often prioritized for testing for novel flu. Adult cases, many of whom are unlikely to seek medical care, are believed more likely to go undetected. H9N2 is ubiquitous in Chinese poultry, and attempts to control the disease via largely ineffective vaccines has led to silent transmission (see NPJ Vaccines: Impact of Inactivated Vaccine on Transmission and Evolution of H9N2 Avian Influenza Virus in Chickens). Complicating matters, as an LPAI (low path avian influenza), H9N2 is not considered a `reportable' disease by WOAH (formerly the OIE), even though it is zoonotic. We've seen seroprevalence studies which suggest people with exposure to infected poultry often develop H9 antibodies, suggesting mild or asymptomatic infection. As a result we are probably only seeing the tip of the H9N2 pyramid, as is true with most infectious diseases in the community. All of which brings us to a new report in One Health, which describes the unexpected finding of an H9N2 infection in an elderly patient already hospitalized for 10 days in Guangzhou for complications from chemotherapy (see timeline below). The patient reportedly had no exposure to poultry, and was only diagnosed because worsening pulmonary function led doctors to order metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of a bronchial lavage sample. It detected both bacterial and H9 viral infection. Of note, subsequent whole gene sequencing (WGS) found several markers linked to mammalian adaptation, including: HA Q226L (human-type receptor binding). PB2 L89V and I292V (increased polymerase activity; I292V also dampens the interferon response). Beyond these findings, this is a reminder of how easily cases can fly under the radar, even those who are already hospitalized for unrelated conditions. First some excerpts from this report, after which I'll have a brief postscript. Severe H9N2 virus infection in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure: implications for surveillance of unexplained severe pneumonia Jingjing Zhang a 1, Weijia Wang b 1, Dan Xia a 1, Yifan Pan c, Yiyun Chen a, Peiwen Liu a, Yuqian Wu a, Anna Wang a, Tengfei Zhou a, Xia Tao a, Shuiping Hou a, Pingting Zhu a, Yanhui Liu a, Xinwei Wu a, Pengzhe Qin a 2, Zhoubin Zhang a 2, Lan Cao a c 2 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.onehlt.2026.101670Get rights and contentView Under a Creative Commons license Open access Highlights • Severe human H9N2 infection detected without known poultry exposure. • Phylogenetic analysis clusters virus with local strains and a recent human case. • Key molecular markers linked to human adaptation of H9N2 identified. • Highlights gaps in current surveillance for sporadic or atypical H9N2 infections Abstract Objectives To describe a severe human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) virus in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure and to evaluate implications for surveillance and public health preparedness. Methods Unbiased metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid for initial pathogen detection, and influenza A(H9N2) virus infection was subsequently confirmed by H9N2-specific real-time RT-PCR. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on H9N2-positive respiratory specimens with sufficient viral RNA, followed by phylogenetic analyses to determine the virus genotype and its genetic relationship with local environmental H9N2 viruses and previously reported human H9N2 viruses. Results The virus, A/Guangzhou/23127/2025 (H9N2), belonged to the G57 genotype, with its HA gene classified within lineage B, clade B4.7, according to the recently proposed global A/H9 classification system. Phylogenetic analysis revealed close genetic relationships with local environmental strains. Conclusion Severe H9N2 infection can occur in individuals without known poultry exposure. These findings underscore the need for NGS-based surveillance among hospitalized patients with severe respiratory disease and highlight the importance of strengthening public health strategies to detect sporadic or atypical zoonotic influenza infections. (SNIP) . . . These findings suggest that H9/H9N2 viruses continued to circulate in local poultry-related environments and that human exposure risk persisted during the study period. However, no human H9N2 infections were identified through routine sentinel surveillance in either hospital-based or occupational monitoring programs during the same period. This discrepancy suggests that current surveillance strategies may not be sufficiently sensitive for detecting sporadic human H9N2 infections, especially among patients without recognized poultry exposure or typical influenza-like illness. (SNIP) In conclusion, this severe human H9N2 infection occurred against a background of continued local environmental circulation and occupational exposure risk. These observations also emphasize the public health importance of sustained environmental surveillance, serological monitoring of occupationally exposed populations, and long-term molecular surveillance of H9N2 viruses. Continued genomic monitoring is particularly important for detecting viral genetic changes associated with mammalian adaptation, including mutations that may affect receptor-binding properties or replication in mammalian hosts. (Continue . . . ) In 2024 the ECDC issued guidance for member nations on Enhanced Influenza Surveillance to Detect Avian Influenza Virus Infections in the EU/EEA During the Inter-Seasonal Period., which cautioned: Sentinel surveillance systems are important for the monitoring of respiratory viruses in the EU/EEA, but these systems are not designed and are not sufficiently sensitive to identify a newly emerging virus such as avian influenza in the general population early enough for the purpose of implementing control measures in a timely way. In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza should be subtyped within 24 hours. How rigorously this is followed isn't known. Last month's Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping focused primarily on testing those with known risk exposures. A sobering reminder that, while we comfort ourselves with our current low number of human novel flu detections, we are probably seeing something less than the whole picture. Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Kentucky: Louisville Zoo Closes Some Bird Exhibits After Stork Dies From Avian Flu Credit Wikipedia #19,419 Over the past 2 months we've seen a steady increase in avian flu reports across the country (and the world), reminding us that levels of environmental HPAI H5 virus are rising, and of our need to take the threat seriously. Canada: CFIA Statement on H5N1 Outbreak At Saskatchewan Poultry Show Oregon ODA Reports Its First Outbreak of HPAI H5 In Dairy Cattle Washington: Hospitalized Avian Flu Case Died - 3rd Case Reported On October 22nd the Louisville Zoo announced the discovery of a sick wild Canada goose on their grounds (see below), which tested presumptively positive for HPAI (H5 assumed, but not specified). It isn't clear from this announcement exactly where on the zoo grounds this goose was found, or even when. First the Zoo's announcement, followed by reports from other sources. Confirmatory testing at a federal lab is pending. None of the Zoo’s birds are currently showing clinical signs of the disease. The Zoo remains open, with temporary closures limited to a handful of bird habitats. supplementary_news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Routine Milk Testing Catches Oregon’s First H5N1 Dairy Case While Union Says Sick Yakima Workers Are Being Missed By Sydney Anderson Published: Nov 17 2026, 12:46 PM EST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Cole Burston | Getty Images Update Note: This article reports new information involving H5N1 bird flu in Pacific Northwest dairy cattle following Nature World News' earlier coverage of Washington's outbreak and the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026. Latest verified updates: Oregon Department of Agriculture confirmation on Nov. 10, 2026; United Farm Workers statements posted Nov. 10–11, 2026; CIDRAP summary of USDA and CDC figures published Nov. 12, 2026. Oregon has confirmed its first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in dairy cattle, at a dairy in Morrow County, after routine statewide milk testing flagged the herd. The Oregon Department of Agriculture said preliminary results came back Nov. 6 and federal confirmation followed Nov. 10. The dairy is under quarantine, and no other affected Oregon dairies have been identified. The detection means the Pacific Northwest dairy cluster now crosses a state line. Across the Columbia River in Washington, the Yakima Valley outbreak has grown to 43 herd detections since Oct. 8, and a farmworker union says the official count of human infections there is far too low. For most households, the practical message has not changed. State and federal officials say pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe. The people facing real risk are different — dairy workers, their families, and anyone drinking raw milk. A Quarantined Morrow County Dairy and a Testing System That Worked Oregon's milk surveillance program tests milk from every licensed dairy operation in the state. The Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University reported the preliminary positive, and samples went to the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories for confirmation. The herd had tested negative consistently before this detection. "Oregon's milk surveillance program worked exactly as intended," said State Veterinarian Dr. Ryan Scholz. The quarantine restricts animal movement, enhanced biosecurity is in place, and an epidemiologic investigation is underway to learn how the virus reached the herd. Officials have not said whether the Oregon case is linked to Washington's outbreak. Farm workers exposed to the infected animals are receiving education and symptom monitoring, according to the Oregon Health Authority. No human cases linked to the Oregon dairy have been identified, and no person-to-person spread has been found. Washington's Outbreak Keeps Growing in the Yakima Valley Washington confirmed its first infected dairy herds on Oct. 8. Since then, detections have climbed to 43 herds, concentrated in Yakima County, according to CIDRAP. Nationally, 51 cattle herds tested positive in the last 30 days, including two in Idaho and the Oregon herd in the past week. Nature World News previously reported that a Yakima County resident exposed to infected dairy cows died of H5N1, the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026. Three human cases have been confirmed in Yakima County, all with occupational exposure to dairy cattle. The CDC counts 74 human H5N1 cases nationwide since 2024, including three deaths. What has changed since that report is the geography and the scrutiny — the virus has now been found in a neighboring state's herd, and the reliability of the human case count is being openly questioned. Union Says the Human Count Is Too Low United Farm Workers posted a series of statements on X on Nov. 10 and 11 saying cases among Yakima Valley dairy workers are being widely undercounted. "We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested," the union said, as reported by Newsweek. The union described symptoms ranging from mild respiratory illness and pinkeye to severe flu-like illness. It linked the gap to fear, saying many workers are immigrants and an ongoing immigration enforcement surge in the valley makes them reluctant to contact public agencies. It also said some workers received only goggles and gloves for handling raw milk, and that instructions on protection have been inconsistent. These are the union's claims, and they have not been independently verified. The union itself reported no signs of human-to-human spread, only workplace exposure to infected animals and milk. Nature World News did not find a public response from the Yakima Health District or the Washington State Department of Health to the union's specific undercount claim in the sources reviewed as of Nov. 16. Milk Remains Safe, but Raw Milk and Farm Work Carry Real Risk Officials are clear on the food supply. USDA said the Oregon detection "does not pose a risk to consumer health or affect the safety of the commercial milk supply." Pasteurization inactivates the virus, and milk from sick animals is barred from the commercial supply. The FDA continues to advise against drinking raw milk. The greater burden falls on dairy workers. "With the use of appropriate personal protective equipment, the risk to farm workers remains low," said Dr. Melissa Sutton, medical director for respiratory viral pathogens at the Oregon Health Authority. That statement depends on workers actually having proper equipment and training, which is the heart of the union's concern. Warning signs for workers include eye redness or irritation, cough, sore throat, fever and body aches after contact with cows or raw milk. Oregon health officials say anyone who develops symptoms should get rapid testing and treatment. Workers who are uncertain where to go can contact their county health department or a community clinic. Next Steps for Families, Workers and Farms For households, the reasonable action is simple. Buy pasteurized milk and dairy products, avoid raw milk, and do not handle sick or dead wild birds. Stopping dairy purchases is unnecessary based on current evidence. Farm owners should report livestock with clinical signs, or unusual sick or dead wildlife, to their state veterinarian. In Oregon, suspected cases in any animal can be reported to ODA at 503-986-4711. Officials will next report results from the Morrow County investigation and any further herd detections through national milk testing. The bottom line: Oregon's first H5N1 dairy case was caught early by routine testing, Washington's outbreak has reached 43 herds, and a union says sick workers are slipping through the cracks. Pasteurized milk remains safe. Whether health agencies expand outreach and testing for Yakima Valley workers is the key question to watch. Related Antarctic Penguin Die-Off First Blamed on Bird Flu Was Mostly Avian Cholera, New Study Finds Bird Flu Reaches Macquarie Island's Elephant Seals as Scientists Brace for a Breeding-Season Die-Off Utah Mink Farm Expects to Lose 80% of Its Animals to Bird Flu, State Records Show What Readers Want to Know Where was Oregon's first H5N1 dairy case found? At a dairy in Morrow County. Preliminary results came Nov. 6, 2026, and USDA confirmed the case Nov. 10. Is pasteurized milk safe to drink? Yes. USDA, FDA and Oregon officials say pasteurization inactivates the virus and the commercial milk supply is safe. Officials advise against drinking raw milk. How many Washington dairy herds are infected? Washington has reported 43 herd detections since Oct. 8, 2026, concentrated in Yakima County. What is the union claiming? United Farm Workers says more Yakima Valley dairy workers are sick with bird flu symptoms than official counts show, partly because fear of immigration enforcement keeps them from seeking testing. The claim has not been independently verified. Who faces the greatest risk? Dairy workers in close contact with infected cows or raw milk face the highest risk. Officials consider the risk to the general public low. What symptoms should dairy workers watch for? Eye redness or irritation, cough, sore throat, fever, and body aches after exposure to cattle or raw milk. Anyone with symptoms should seek rapid testing and treatment. © 2026 NatureWorldNews.com All rights reserved. Do not reproduce without permission. Prev Next Health experts warn that the simultaneous circulation of bird flu and seasonal influenza could increase the risk of a new virus capable of spreading between humans. (Scripps News) By: Jay Gray Posted 12:54 AM, Nov 14, 2026 Share Copy linkFacebookNextdoorXThreadsRedditLinkedInEmailWhatsAppMessengerPrint Add Scripps News as a Google Preferred Source Health experts warn that the simultaneous circulation of bird flu and seasonal influenza could increase the risk of a new virus capable of spreading between humans. A growing bird flu outbreak across the United States is raising concerns among public health experts, as infections spread through dairy cattle and poultry flocks and scientists warn about the potential for the virus to evolve. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE The H5N1 virus is being blamed for at least one human death in Washington state, where the outbreak has been particularly severe. But health officials may not know the full extent of human infections. The United Farm Workers union warns that increased immigration enforcement could discourage agricultural workers from reporting possible infections or seeking assistance from public health agencies. "Given the current and ongoing ICE surge ... many or most of the workers are understandably reluctant to proactively engage with public agencies," the union said in a social media post. RELATED STORY | Bird flu detected in California elephant seals for first time According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, H5N1 infections have been confirmed in dairy cattle herds in six states over the past 30 days. The virus has also been detected in backyard and commercial poultry flocks across 17 states during that period. While the outbreak has raised concerns about human exposure, particularly among people who work closely with infected animals, there is currently no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission of H5N1. However, scientists warn that could change. Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, director of Brown University's Pandemic Center, says scientists have been concerned about H5N1 for decades. "This H5N1 virus has been the top of our future pandemic worry list for a really long time, for 25 years," Nuzzo said. One of the biggest concerns is the overlap between the ongoing bird flu outbreak and the start of the traditional influenza season. As seasonal flu infections increase, scientists worry about the possibility of avian and human influenza viruses infecting the same host and exchanging genetic material. "When you have a whole lot of bird virus circulating, at the same time that you have a whole lot of human virus circulating, it just raises worries that those two viruses are gonna find each other and swap genes," Nuzzo explained. That process, known as genetic reassortment, could potentially produce a new influenza virus with characteristics that make it more dangerous to humans. Nuzzo says the worst-case scenario would be the emergence of a virus that people have little or no immunity against and that can spread easily from person to person. RELATED STORY | Pet owners urged to watch for screwworm as cases emerge in dogs For now, H5N1 remains primarily an animal health threat, with human infections generally associated with exposure to infected animals. But the continued spread of the virus among dairy cattle and poultry creates additional opportunities for human exposure and viral evolution. Scientists are closely monitoring those developments, particularly as seasonal influenza begins circulating more widely. Advertisement Updated: 6:11 PM CST Nov 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jonathan Greco Digital Media Manager ﻿﻿﻿Highly pathogenic avian influenza case confirmed in Oklahoma dairy herd Updated: 6:11 PM CST Nov 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jonathan Greco Digital Media Manager OKLAHOMA CITY — State officials announced that the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service confirmed a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in an Oklahoma dairy herd. >> Open the video player above to see some of the headlines KOCO 5 is following. Advertisement Details about the dairy herd and where in Oklahoma the avian influenza case was found have not been released. Highly pathogenic avian influenza in Oklahoma Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry officials told KOCO 5 that this is an isolated incident and there is no concern about safety of pasteurized milk or dairy products. The commercial milk supply remains safe due to federal animal health requirements and pasteurization. "This is a reportable disease that we see from time to time and is not a cause for alarm," Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry said in a statement to KOCO 5. Authorities say dairy farmers should remain vigilant for signs of highly pathogenic avian influenza. Those signs include: A decline in feed intake A decrease in milk yield A drop in rumination Thicker, concentrated, colostrum-like milk Dehydration Fever Dairy farmers who suspect a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza should call the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry as soon as possible at 405-522-6141. More information about disease alerts can be found here . Avian Influenza Avian influenza, which is better known as bird flu , is a contagious viral disease of domestic and wild birds. USDA officials say it's a major threat to the poultry industry, animal health, trade, and the economy worldwide. The bird flu varies in severity depending on the strain and species affected, according to the USDA. Highly pathogenic avian influenza strains are deadly to domestic poultry and can wipe out entire flocks in a matter of days. Symptoms of highly pathogenic avian influenza are: Sudden death without any prior symptoms of illness Lack of energy and appetite A drop in egg production or soft-shelled, misshapen eggs Swelling of the eyelids, comb, wattles, and shanks Purple discoloration of the wattles, comb, and legs Gasping for air (difficulty breathing) Nasal discharge, coughing, sneezing Twisting of the head and neck (torticollis) Stumbling or falling down Diarrhea The USDA says there's no treatment for highly pathogenic avian influenza, and the only way to stop the disease is to depopulate all affected and exposed poultry. >> Download the KOCO 5 App | Subscribe to KOCO 5’s YouTube channel | Sign up for KOCO 5’s Morning Newsletter Make KOCO a preferred source on Google Add Preferred Source Infinite Scroll Enabled Top Picks Oklahoma City homes vandalized with Nazi symbols and spray-painted cameras Emergency crews on scene of 'major traffic accident' in Stillwater, fire department says Oklahoma Highway Patrol makes arrest in fatal hit-and-run near Stillwater Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised in cyberattack SPONSORED CONTENT Men Over 40 Are Ditching The Blue Pill for This 7x Stronger Alternative HartfordReviewJournal 23 Cool Gadgets Selling out This Month Consumer Trail 1 Simple Hack to Save on Your Electric Bill (Try Tonight) HomeWise Journal The Real Reason Most Seniors End Up Using a Walker and How to Avoid It ApexLabs Powered By Revcontent

supplementary_news.content: Toggle search form Search for: Toggle navigation Oklahoma Farm Report Home Listen to Us Markets Ag News Ag News Agri-Innovations Blue Green Gazette Weather Calendar Auctions Daily Emails Daily Emails Archives Subscribe to Daily Email About Us About Us Our Team Oklahoma Farm Report Radio Affiliates Beef Buzz Contact Contact Us Advertise With Us Email Us a Story/Idea/Content Cow-Calf Corner Dr Peel: Understanding Steer-Heifer Price Differences House Democratic Caucus Leadership Team for First Regular Session of the 61st Legislature Nov 16 USDA Confirms Case of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in an Oklahoma Dairy Herd The United States Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) has confirmed a case of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in an Oklahoma dairy herd. While this detection marks an important development for the state’s livestock industry, state and federal officials emphasize that the commercial milk supply remains safe. According to agricultural officials, there is no concern regarding the safety of pasteurized milk or dairy products. Federal animal health requirements, combined with the standard pasteurization process, ensure that commercial dairy products remain safe for consumers. In response to the confirmation, the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry (ODAFF) is urging Oklahoma dairy farmers to remain vigilant, enhance their biosecurity protocols and practices, and communicate regularly with their herd veterinarians. Producers should closely monitor their herds for clinical signs of HPAI, which include: A decline in feed intake A decrease in milk yield A drop in rumination Thicker, concentrated, colostrum-like milk Dehydration Fever HPAI is a serious, highly contagious disease that requires a rapid response—particularly because it is often fatal to chickens and poses a significant threat to poultry operations alongside dairy herds. If an Oklahoma dairy farmer suspects a case of HPAI in their herd, they are urged to report it to ODAFF as soon as possible by calling 405-522-6141. For general questions regarding HPAI, a 2-1-1 phone line is currently active and available 24 hours a day. If operators on the 2-1-1 line are unable to answer a specific question, they will connect the caller directly with an ODAFF employee for assistance. Additional educational resources, biosecurity recommendations for dairy farms, testing guidelines for lactating dairy cattle at exhibitions, and guidance from organizations such as Oklahoma State Extension, the FDA, the USDA’s Defend the Flock program, and the National Milk Producers Federation are available through ODAFF to help producers and the public stay informed. Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza – is a serious disease and requires rapid response because it is highly contagious and often fatal to chickens. ODAFF Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Overview Handout Guidance for Hunters on how to Protect Yourself and Birds from HPAI USDA’s Defend the Flock Resources Questions and Answers Regarding the Safety of Eggs During Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Outbreaks | FDA Oklahoma State Extension HPAI Overview Youtube Recording of HPAI Webinar (May 2, 2022) HPAI IN DAIRY CATTLE Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) has been confirmed in dairy cattle in several states. There is no concern about the safety of pasteurized milk or dairy products. The commercial milk supply remains safe due to both federal animal health requirements and pasteurization. It is recommended that Oklahoma dairy farmers enhance their biosecurity protocols and practices, communicate regularly with their herd veterinarian, and report any possible HPAI cases to ODAFF by calling 405-522-6141. The order came into force on 13 November following an outbreak of avian flu. It means anyone who gives away or sells eggs or poultry products, as well as those who keep 50 or more birds, must keep the animals indoors. "I don't know whether we will continue or whether this might be the end of free-range turkeys as such," said Margaret Warmington, who co-owns Ireley Farm in Winchcombe, Gloucestershire. "You feel a bit fraudulent saying free-range, and people want to pay extra for having free-range which it isn't then, so you know they could go down to their local supermarket and just buy something," added Warmington, who rears turkeys as well as other livestock. More from Gloucestershire Murder investigation launched after man's death Couple banned from owning pets after kitten deaths Gymshark legal battle costs small gym thousands Pete Benn, who runs Bisley Birds in Stroud, Gloucestershire, said farmers could still call their birds free-range whilst under lockdown. "If bird flu restrictions are in force those birds can be housed indefinitely and they never lose their free-range status," he said. "Most people have a coop but they'll want to look at having a covered run as well so that the chickens can still have access to outdoor areas," said Benn. Some honesty box egg sellers have also stopped egg sales whilst the lockdown continues. "Even if you just give an egg to your neighbour, just over the wall, it's still classed as given away," Benn added. Simon Small is limiting visitors to his poultry farm near Glastonbury Avian influenza is a bigger issue in the east of the country, in places like Lincolnshire and Norfolk. "At the moment there's nothing in this area so [it's] not too bad but you just do not want it in the area," explained Simon Small who owns a turkey farm near Glastonbury in Somerset. "Any reported cases of bird flu are a long distance from us so we've just got to keep our fingers crossed." Small's farm is now limiting the number of visitors to help protect the birds. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, near Chard has also put measures in place following the lockdown announcement. A spokesperson for the charity said: "Our fantastic estates team were already one step ahead, having prepared a lovely space for our feathered friends back in late summer, ready for just such an occasion. "Although they won't have access to the pond, the team will make sure they have a paddling pool to enjoy instead." Another wildlife sanctuary, WWT Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, has also made precautions for the safety of its flocks. A spokesperson said: "We have temporarily suspended public bird feeding to protect our birds from illness. "There will be no bird seed available today, but you can watch a commentated wild bird feed from the Peng Observatory." Follow BBC Gloucestershire on Facebook, X and Instagram. rationale GTA VI’s record day Stock market today Cal-Maine Foods Reports Avian Influenza Outbreak at Florida Facility Affecting 1.76 Million Birds Fiona Craig Wed, November 18, 2026 at 8:39 AM CST 2 min read CALM Flock of chickens ©Adobe Stock Images Cal-Maine Foods, Inc. (NASDAQ:CALM) announced that one of its egg production facilities in Florida has tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), resulting in the planned removal of approximately 1.76 million birds from its flock. In a statement issued on November 18, 2026, the US egg producer confirmed that the outbreak would require the depopulation of approximately 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, representing around 2.7% of its total flock. Production at the affected facility has been temporarily suspended while the company implements disease control and containment procedures established by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). Cal-Maine Implements Containment Measures and Adjusts Production Cal-Maine Foods said it is following the USDA's prescribed protocols in response to the confirmed infection, including the depopulation of birds at the affected location. The company is also coordinating production and distribution activities across its other facilities to maintain egg supplies and minimise disruption to customers. These operational adjustments are intended to offset the temporary loss of production capacity at the Florida facility while containment measures remain in place. Although the affected birds account for approximately 2.7% of Cal-Maine's total flock, the company has not provided a specific estimate of the outbreak's financial impact or the expected duration of the production suspension. Health Authorities Maintain Low Risk Assessment for General Public The company referred to guidance from US health and agricultural authorities regarding the risks associated with highly pathogenic avian influenza. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the risk to the general US population from HPAI viruses is currently considered low. The USDA has also stated that avian influenza cannot be transmitted through eggs that have been safely handled and properly cooked. Cal-Maine confirmed that no eggs have been recalled as a result of HPAI. The company's response remains focused on containing the outbreak, complying with federal disease management requirements and maintaining continuity of supply. Further Information Expected in Next SEC Quarterly Filing Cal-Maine Foods indicated that it plans to provide additional information about the outbreak in its next quarterly report filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The company does not expect to issue interim updates unless developments are considered material. Story Continues The outbreak represents a temporary operational disruption for the egg producer, with the extent of any financial or production impact dependent on the containment process and the company's ability to redistribute supply across its remaining facilities. Investors will be monitoring the company's next regulatory filing for further details on the incident and any resulting effects on its operations. Louisville Zoo stork dies of bird flu, mate of nearly 30 years euthanized WLKY US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 0:32 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 6:36 PM EST Nov 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Alex Suckow Digital Media Manager Louisville Zoo stork dies of bird flu, mate euthanized; several exhibits closed Updated: 6:36 PM EST Nov 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Alex Suckow Digital Media Manager LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Two birds at the Louisville Zoo have died. The zoo announced Monday that a 28-year-old female European white stork named Awan was found dead inside her exhibit on Nov. 11. Awan tested positive for avian influenza, or bird flu. Advertisement Her enclosure mate, a 27-year-old male named Cain, then showed signs of bird flu, too, and was euthanized days later, on Sunday. Cain's results are pending. “Awan and Cain have been together here at the Zoo for nearly 30 years. Losing them so suddenly is deeply felt by the animal care keeper teams who have known and cared for them over the years,” said Dan Maloney, Louisville Zoo director. This is the first time an animal in the zoo's bird collection has tested positive for bird flu, the zoo said. Around three weeks ago, the zoo found a wild Canada goose on its grounds with the flu, and implemented safety measures, including closing some bird exhibits. But they did eventually reopen. | Read more here. In response to this new case, the zoo said it is implementing those closures again and adding biosecurity measures. Public walk-through aviaries, including Lorikeet Landing in Australia, the Forest Bird Trail and African penguin exhibits in the Islands Pavilion, the Steller’s Sea Eagle Aviary in Glacier Run, and areas around the zoo lake will remain closed until the threat has cleared. Select birds will also be moved indoors as a precaution, including the flamingo flock, two American bald eagles, the little penguins, and others. The zoo said staff and veterinary teams are taking enhanced precautions, including continuous monitoring of all native and collection birds on zoo grounds. Animal care staff are also following strict biosecurity protocols, including the use of disinfecting footbaths or dedicated boot covers for select animal holding areas, and staff designated exclusively for either indoor or outdoor bird care. “Our crews are trained and prepared to respond to emerging health concerns. Protecting the animals in our care is at the heart of what we do every day, and we are committed to these additional measures as we respond to the current avian influenza threat," Maloney said. Other animal schedules will remain flexible while the zoo follows its current biosecurity protocols.
